tip: 'Kaki lima' = street vendors, named after the five-foot walkway ('kaki lima') they occupy.
'Bukan main' = 'no joke', unbelievably: 'pedasnya bukan main' = it is seriously spicy.
'Garing' and 'renyah' both mean crispy: 'garing' for fried-dry crunch, 'renyah' for fresh crunch.
'Setengah matang' = half-cooked: soft-boiled eggs, rare steak. 'Matang' = cooked/ripe.
Cooking talk loves 'di-' verbs: 'dikukus' = steamed, 'digoreng' = fried, 'direbus' = boiled.
'Sedangkan' contrasts two subjects: 'ayah lebih suka ikan bakar, sedangkan saya suka ikan goreng' = Dad prefers grilled fish, while I like fried fish.
'Sedikit demi sedikit' = little by little; 'demi' repeats units: 'satu demi satu' = one by one.
'Ayam kampung' is literally 'village chicken' – free-range birds that roam the 'kampung', pricier but 'lebih gurih'. Ordinary farmed chicken is 'ayam negeri' or broiler.
'Diungkep' is a specific kitchen step: simmered slowly in the spice paste so 'bumbunya meresap' (the seasoning soaks in). 'Direbus' is just boiling in water and wouldn't get the seasoning in.
English 'rice' splits in two: 'beras' is the raw grain you buy, 'nasi' is cooked rice on the plate. 'Lontong' starts from 'beras', then cooks inside the banana leaf.
Grilling is 'bakar', not 'masak': 'membakar ikan' = to grill fish; 'masak' = cooking in general.
The ending '-nya' makes a quality the topic: 'pedasnya level berapa?' = how spicy is it (its spiciness, what level)?
'Tidak kuat' + something = can't handle it: 'saya tidak kuat pedas' = I can't take spice.
'Pun' attaches after the word it stresses: 'level lima pun' = even level five. Paired with 'masih kurang' it builds the common 'even X still isn't enough' shape.
'Ke-...-an' here = overcome by: 'kepedasan' = too spicy to handle, 'kepanasan' = overheated.
The 'warung' question: 'makan di sini atau dibungkus?' = for here or to go? 'Bungkus' = wrap up, take away.
'Warteg' ('warung Tegal') = cheap point-and-choose rice stalls named after the town of Tegal.
'Warung' custom: you eat first and settle up after. 'Bayarnya nanti saja di kasir' = just pay later at the register – you're not expected to pay before eating.
'Tukang' + food = the seller: 'tukang sate' = satay man, 'tukang bakso' pushes his cart around.
The 'soto' question at the counter: 'dicampur' (rice in the bowl) or 'dipisah' (rice on the side)?
The ending '-kan' can mean doing it for someone: 'ambilkan' = fetch (for you).
'Selagi' = while it lasts: 'selagi masih panas' = while it is still hot.
'Baru' here = only then: 'baru mau makan' = will only eat (once the condition is met).
'Saya bagian' + task = it's my department: 'saya bagian cuci piring' = I handle the dishes.
'Turun-temurun' = handed down through the generations ('turun' = to descend).
'Tinggal' + verb = all that's left to do: 'tinggal pesan' = just order.
'Sekalian' = while we're at it, all together: 'sekalian sama es tehnya' = including the iced tea.
'Biar' = casual 'supaya' (so that): 'biar gampang' = so it's easy.
'Porsi bungkus' = takeaway portion; Padang stalls famously give extra rice when you 'bungkus'.
'Ada yang ..., ada yang ...' = some ..., others ...: 'ada yang suka, ada yang tidak tahan' = some like it, some can't stand it.
